theme: Give the king your justice, the ideal reign
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 72. It is a prayer for the king, and the only psalm attributed to Solomon in this section. Notice how much it says about justice for the poor, and how widely the king’s rule extends.
settingTheScene: The title says, “Of Solomon,” and the last line says, “The prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are ended.” It may be a prayer by David for his son, or a prayer for Solomon at his accession. It closes Book II of the Psalter. The psalm describes what a king should be, and in doing so, reaches far beyond anything Solomon could achieve. It describes the Messiah.
observation: “Give the king your justice, O God, and your righteousness to the royal son!” (v. 1).
“May he judge your people with righteousness, and your poor with justice!” (v. 2).
“May he defend the cause of the poor of the people, give deliverance to the children of the needy, and crush the oppressor!” (v. 4).
“May they fear you while the sun endures, and as long as the moon, throughout all generations!” (v. 5).
“May he be like rain that falls on the mown grass, like showers that water the earth!” (v. 6).
“May he have dominion from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth!” (v. 8).
“For he delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper” (v. 12).
“May his name endure forever, his fame continue as long as the sun! May people be blessed in him, all nations call him blessed!” (v. 17).
interpretation:
The prayer begins with a request that the king would have God’s own justice. The king does not make justice. He receives it from God. A good ruler is one who reflects the character of the LORD. And the first test of justice, in this psalm, is how the poor are treated. The king is called to defend the poor, deliver the needy, and crush the oppressor. The word “poor” appears again and again. In the Bible, a ruler’s quality is measured by what happens to the weakest.

The next image is a beautiful one: the king’s rule as rain on mown grass. After the harvest, the field is cut short and dry, and rain brings new growth. A righteous king revives the land. Justice brings flourishing.

The psalm’s scope is large. “From sea to sea.” “To the ends of the earth.” “Kings bow down to him.” This is a vision of universal rule, and it reflects the promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). In the last verses, we hear the promise echoed: “May people be blessed in him, all nations call him blessed!”

Solomon’s reign did not match this ideal. It began with promise, but it ended in oppression, taxation, and idolatry. The psalm remained a prayer waiting for an answer. The people kept praying for the king who would fulfill it.

The final doxology, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things,” closes the second book of the Psalms. It leaves the reader with the sense that this prayer is not finished. “May the whole earth be filled with his glory! Amen and Amen!”
connection: Jesus is the king who defends the poor (Luke 4:18; 6:20), who delivers the needy who cry to him, and whose rule will reach “from sea to sea.” The wise men from the East brought gifts and bowed down (Matthew 2:11). Philippians 2:10-11 says every knee will bow. Galatians 3:8 shows the blessing of Abraham reaching the nations. Revelation 21:24-26 pictures the kings of the earth bringing glory into the city.
application:
Ask how you treat the poor, the needy, and those without influence. What does the psalm ask of you?

Pray this psalm for the leaders of your nation, and for the reign of Christ.

Pray “May the whole earth be filled with his glory” for a specific place or people.
prayerPrompts: Pray for justice for the poor and needy.
Pray that all nations would come to know him.
